title: The Best/Worst of Reddit Fitness - The Ten Commandments of Lifting
summary: NH reviews a top r/fitness post listing ten 'commandments' of lifting, finding most of it decent if obvious, with some pseudo-scientific myths (cardio causing insulin resistance, post-workout window, no protein/fat after training). He argues the list over-focuses on nutrition and gimmicks while barely mentioning training, which is the true priority.
claims: Carbs are not the enemy; tolerance depends on the individual's digestion, body fat and ethnic background
Base your diet on your ancestry and what your ancestors had access to, plus how your body responds; it avoids problems down the line
Carbs are for champions: you should earn your carbs; most people eat pasta, rice and bread calories they don't need
He eats carbs only on training days, originally to cut and now as discipline so he never skips a session
Carbs can cause inflammation in certain people
Sleeping 10-12 hours like elite performers is unrealistic and overkill for most; 7-8 hours is what most working people can and should get
Oversleeping can leave you sluggish and feeling worse with no gain in recovery
Sleep is as important as, if not more important than, diet for recovery; he avoids caffeine to protect it
There is no hard rule like 72 hours between sessions for a muscle; 24 or 48 hours works if you manage volume and intensity, e.g. a lighter first session
Constantly rotating exercises makes you relearn movement patterns and stall; variation is fine only if it stays specific to the key lifts
Thinking in 'heavy days' is a powerlifting mindset; you should just have training days with intensity and volume varied within them
'The best diet is the one you stick to' only holds if the diet is healthy; people can stick to frozen pizza and beer for 15 years and then die
Bodybuilding nutrition need not be bland chicken and broccoli; he eats a diverse diet with fats and sodium, restricting sugars except from fruit
Avoiding processed food and snacks matters most for overweight people; otherwise snacking within your macros is fine
Static stretching before training is mostly a waste of time; real mobility comes from lifting through full range with weights, stretching is only a supplement
Cardio before weights is a bad idea because it reduces your intensity on the lifts; the best warm-up for lifting is lifting lighter weights
Potentiation just means warming up with the same lift at light weight to fire the nervous system, lubricate joints and fill the muscle with blood; elaborate timed protocols are a waste
Upper back rounding on the deadlift comes from a weak or unstable lower back and poor technique, not a weak upper back; stability starts at the hips, glutes and core
The upper back is mostly a stabilizer in the squat and deadlift, not a prime mover
Never do light high-rep work (like 4x25 with no rest) before your main strength sets; it steals energy and reps from the main work and does nothing for hypertrophy
High-rep light work can help strong powerlifters regain strength they previously had, but cannot build strength that was never there
Natural lifters eating normally don't need to think about insulin sensitivity; that obsession comes from enhanced pros using insulin
Walking is essential for health; when he was very heavy with 400 lb squats he couldn't walk 15 minutes without ankle pain and breathlessness
Losing the ability to walk is a sign health markers are declining and you're packing on too much mass; keep calisthenics in your training
Walk up stairs on your toes daily and your calves will grow over time
He spends 30-minute breaks walking shirtless outside in the sun for movement and vitamin D
Cardio just means getting your heart rate up; any method works, even jumping jacks, treadmills and steppers are not mandatory
The claim that long slow distance work inhibits muscle growth and fat loss is nonsense; it could only limit growth through calorie shortfall
He prefers HIIT because it saves time and is more fun; sprints, beep tests or giant sets work well
The most dangerous thing for beginners is bad ideas that get them hurt or make them quit, like believing kipping 'butterfly' pull-ups build more muscle
The neck is a muscle and neck training is legitimate; people mocking neck curls often have pencil necks
Most gym bros train only mirror muscles, leading to shoulder pain from weak rear delts and traps and lower back pain from poor thoracic integrity
The posterior chain must be a priority across compounds and dedicated days, not just in accessory selection; a big back, glutes and hamstrings are also aesthetic
Treat your upper back like a slave: throw volume at it with good form and progression; four sets of lat pulldown won't build big lats
Salt is not bad for you; demonizing it causes cramps and poor hydration, as water without minerals just passes through (clear urine)
A home-cooked whole-food diet is low in salt, so you should salt your food
Salt is a baseline need, not the single biggest performance factor; fixing a deficiency just restores normal function
Nutrition, hydration and recovery are essential background conditions, but training is the most important thing for results
Supercompensation happens over the period of protein synthesis after training; you have about 24 hours and prior meals already supply nutrients, so there is no urgent post-workout window
Missing a meal or waiting two hours after training won't hurt recovery unless it becomes chronic; the urgency myth is sold by supplement companies
A sugary post-workout drink like orange juice is optional and mostly placebo
The idea that protein or fat right after training slows absorption is nonsense, comparable to the old myth that eating after training pulls blood away from muscles
As a 14-year-old he was told by older men not to eat after training because blood would leave the muscles, and he believed it
Fitness suffers from 'microcosmic hyperfocus': people fixate on one gimmick like salt because fixing a deficiency gave them a big jump
He would keep only about 20% of the list in his own ten commandments; it over-focuses on nutrition and barely covers training
exercises: does not build more muscle despite internet claims
the neck is a muscle that benefits from training
walk up stairs on your toes daily
four sets alone won't build big lats; upper back needs much more volume
mobility with weights beats static stretching
